debate.situation: You are asking why places like coastal Norway or Britain have much milder winters than parts of Canada at about the same latitude. The common answer credits the Gulf Stream, but you have not said whether you want the single biggest cause or the full set of causes. That matters, because the popular answer may be partly right yet incomplete, and how much each factor counts is still debated.

minds.title: The Gulf Stream Advocate
minds.concern: Ocean currents carry tropical heat north, and that visible, measurable transport should be credited first.
minds.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
minds.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea

minds.title: The Wind and Weather Analyst
minds.concern: Heat only reaches land through the air, so prevailing winds and the contrast between sea and land decide who is warm.
minds.author: Hubert Lamb
minds.book: Climate, History and the Modern World

minds.title: The Counterexample Hunter
minds.concern: A tidy cause should be tested against cases that could break it, and a story that explains everything may explain nothing.
minds.author: Karl Popper

debate.speaker: The Gulf Stream Advocate
debate.text: It is the Gulf Stream, plain and simple. A great river of warm water leaves the tropics and runs up toward Europe, and the air above it is gently heated all winter. Norway is warm because the ocean is delivering heat there, and Labrador gets no such delivery.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Counterexample Hunter
debate.text: Then here is a case that could sink you. Vancouver sits near fifty degrees north on the Pacific side of Canada, with no Gulf Stream, and it is mild in winter. If your cause is necessary, Vancouver should be frozen. Is it?
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.speaker: The Gulf Stream Advocate
debate.text: Fair hit. I will narrow my claim. The Pacific has its own warm current too, so I would say currents help both coasts. But I still say the Atlantic one is stronger and carries more heat to Europe.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Wind and Weather Analyst
debate.text: You are both skipping the middle step. A current does not heat Norway directly. Westerly winds blow across the ocean, pick up its stored warmth, and carry it ashore. Stand on the east side of a continent and the same winds blow off cold land, so the heat never arrives.
debate.author: Hubert Lamb
debate.book: Climate, History and the Modern World
debate.basis: Basis: Hubert Lamb, Climate, History and the Modern World

debate.speaker: The Gulf Stream Advocate
debate.text: So the wind is a delivery truck and my current is the warehouse. Without my warehouse, the truck arrives empty. You cannot call that a minor role.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Wind and Weather Analyst
debate.text: The warehouse is the whole ocean, not one current. Water holds heat far better than land does. It stores summer warmth and releases it in winter, so any coast downwind of a big ocean stays mild. I would go further than Lamb here and say that storage may matter more than the transport you love.
debate.author: Hubert Lamb
debate.book: Climate, History and the Modern World
debate.basis: Basis: Hubert Lamb, Climate, History and the Modern World

debate.speaker: The Counterexample Hunter
debate.text: That gives us a test. If storage and wind are the main story, then a coast with the Gulf Stream moved away should still be mild, and an inland place should still be cold even beside a warm current. A claim that survives those tests earns more trust than one nobody can threaten.
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.speaker: The Gulf Stream Advocate
debate.text: Then I will concede the wind and the storage, but not the whole case. Eastern Canada is also washed by a cold current coming down from the north. That is an ocean effect too, and it chills the coast that your westerlies leave exposed.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Wind and Weather Analyst
debate.text: Agreed, and it strengthens the pattern. Canada's east gets cold air flowing off a huge frozen continent, and a cold current on top of that. Europe gets the opposite on both counts. The contrast is real, but the sizes of each piece are still argued over, and I will not pretend otherwise.
debate.author: Hubert Lamb
debate.book: Climate, History and the Modern World
debate.basis: Basis: Hubert Lamb, Climate, History and the Modern World

debate.speaker: The Counterexample Hunter
debate.text: One more caution for both of you. Saying the Gulf Stream explains it is easy to remember, which is why it spreads. Easy to remember is not the same as well tested. The honest answer is a bundle of causes with uncertain weights, and a good answer says that.
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the warmth of northern Europe is probably not one cause but a chain: warm ocean water, the sea storing heat, and westerly winds carrying that heat ashore, set against cold continental air and a cold current on Canada's east side. The Vancouver case suggests the Gulf Stream alone cannot be the whole story. What stays disputed is how much each link contributes. A possible self-reflection is whether you wanted a single headline cause or a picture of how the pieces fit together.
debate.dependsOn: If you want a quick, defensible answer, then say that ocean heat storage and prevailing westerly winds, helped by warm currents, keep Europe mild, because that matches the Vancouver case as well. If you care about which factor is largest, then the answer depends on the size of the Gulf Stream's heat transport compared with the effect of wind and storage, which is still debated, so check recent climate science rather than relying on one account. If you want to test the explanation yourself, compare winter temperatures for coastal and inland places on the same latitude on both sides of the Atlantic and the Pacific, and see whether wind direction and distance from the ocean predict the pattern better than currents alone.
